Wang Zhen says: According to ancient accounts, a one-<term>mu</term> <gloss>traditional land measure</gloss> plot for <term>qu-tian</term> <gloss>pitted fields</gloss> is fifteen paces wide. With each pace measured at five feet, this equals seventy-five feet. Each row occupies one foot five inches, dividing the width into fifty rows. The length is sixteen paces, which equals eighty feet. Allowing one foot five inches per row along the length, this divides into fifty-four rows. Multiplying the length and width yields two thousand seven hundred pits in total.

Leave alternating rows empty, planting only within the designated rows. Within each planted row, skip every other pit, planting one pit and leaving the next empty. Setting aside the empty spaces, six hundred and seventy-five pits may be planted. Each pit is one foot deep. Blend one <term>sheng</term> <gloss>volume measure of roughly one liter</gloss> of cured manure with the soil of the pit. Scatter the seed evenly and cover it, pressing down firmly by hand so that the seeds adhere closely to the soil.

When seedlings emerge, inspect their density and thin them accordingly. Hoeing can never be done too frequently. Water the plot in dry weather. When seeds begin to set, hoe the soil deeply and bank it firmly around the roots to protect against swaying from strong winds. The ancients sowed their crops according to this method, harvesting one <term>dou</term> <gloss>measure of roughly ten liters</gloss> of grain from each pit, each

<summary>Wang Zhen explains the precise dimensions, pit layout, and spacing calculations for cultivating a one-mu plot under the pitted field method. The text specifies methods for fertilization, firming the soil, thinning seedlings, frequent hoeing, watering, and mounding soil around the roots to secure high yields and guard against wind damage.</summary>

Lü Dalin said: A benevolent person regards all under Heaven as one single body. When ailments, sores, aches, and itches occur, that which stirs our hearts with sorrow, grief, alarm, and trepidation is not something produced by calculated intelligence or deliberate effort. Because one regards all under Heaven as one single body, there is not a single person or a single creature that is not part of one's own form. Therefore, embracing all under Heaven is the way to unite our love. Thus, in a year of bad harvests and famine, when the cereal crops do not mature and the common people bear the look of starvation, the state ruler, high officials, and ordinary officers all share in their distress. It is not that the ruler is incapable of royal dining, nor that the high officials and officers lack estates and stipends; rather, the heart of a benevolent person shares this in common with the people, so that even when eating, he cannot feel full. And when it comes to having nine years of stored reserves, even in the event of severe drought or flooding...

<summary>Citing the Book of Rites and scholar Lü Dalin, the text explains how rulers and officials must restrict their meals, rituals, and luxuries during famine to share hardship with the people, regarding all subjects as part of their own physical body.</summary>
<keywords>Book of Rites, Quli, Lü Dalin, benevolence, famine relief, self-restraint, Confucian governance</keywords>

## Making Fish Preserves, Number Seventy-Four

Whenever making <term>zha</term> <gloss>fermented fish preserve</gloss>, spring and autumn are the proper seasons; winter and summer are unsuitable.
In cold weather it matures with difficulty; in hot weather it will not succeed unless heavily salted.
If heavily salted, it loses its flavor, and furthermore will breed maggots; it is better not to make
fermented fish
at all.

Take fresh carp.
The fish should only be large to be good; lean fish are even better. Fat ones, though delicious, do not keep
long. Those with flesh one and a half feet or more in length, whose skin and bones are hard and tough and unsuitable for raw slices,
are all well suited for
fermented fish preserve.

When descaling is completed, slice the meat into strips. The shape of each strip should be two inches long, one inch wide, and five tenths of an inch thick. Ensure that every
strip individually retains skin.

If the strips are too large and long, the exterior will be over-fermented and damaged by vinegar, rendering it unfit for eating before the center becomes edible.
The flesh near the bone remains raw and fishy, inedible; typically only one part in three can be salvaged. If the strips are small, they
ripen evenly. The inch measurements given are merely a general guideline; one must not be rigidly bound by them. The backbone should be chopped square. Where the flesh is thick,

Eighth, they say that the three substances are distinct while their characteristic is one. This formulation is devised precisely to rescue their position from the preceding objection.

If they claim that the three entities are distinct in substance yet identical in characteristic, they directly contradict their own doctrine that substance and characteristic are one.

This contradicts their own tenet that substance is identical to characteristic. Formulating a syllogism based on the identity and difference of substance and characteristic, we state: "Your original three entities should have no distinction in substance, because you assert that substance and characteristic have no distinction; just like the produced characteristic."

Alternatively: "The characteristics should be threefold and distinct, because they are not distinct from the substances; just like the three original substances."

Because they accept that the characteristic is one while the entities are three, they contradict their own school, since their school maintains that the three substances are the characteristics. They should not be simultaneously three and one. This contradiction of their own doctrine forms one objection.

From here down, the ninth and tenth syllogisms state:

"Substance should be indistinctly one, just like characteristic; and characteristic should be distinctly three, just like substance. Therefore, one should not assert..."

### Method for Preparing the Supreme Treasure of the First Menses

Take the authentic first menses obtained at five thousand and forty-eight days <note>this count corresponds to approximately fourteen years of age, the traditional onset of puberty and fertility</note>, whether collected in a vessel or on silk. Wash it down with one bowl of freshly discharged boy's urine <term>tongbian</term> <gloss>urine from a healthy young boy</gloss>. Add ten bowls of clear water, introduce one <term>qian</term> <gloss>approximately 3.7 grams</gloss> of alum, and stir one hundred to one hundred and ten times. Once it has settled, decant and discard the clear water. Change the water again with ten bowls of clear water, stir to clarify as before, and decant the clear water completely. Add one <term>zhong</term> <gloss>small cup</gloss> of fresh breast milk from a woman who has given birth to her firstborn son. Place them together into a metal vessel, seal it with three or four layers of pasted paper, and place it in the sunlight to dry in the sun for three days. Alternatively, seal the mouth of the vessel with clay, place it in an ash vat, and nourish it over a small crown fire <note>gentle heat applied from above</note> for three days. Take it out and grind it into a fine powder.

<summary>This page concludes the drying of purified Red Lead and presents the recipe for the Supreme Treasure of the First Menses. The menstrual substance is washed with boy's urine, clarified repeatedly with alum water, combined with breast milk in a metal vessel, and cured either by sunlight or gentle fire over three days before being reduced to powder.</summary>

There are also wild silkworm cocoons, which are formed by wild silkworms living on mulberry trees. Every district collects them, but only the people of Shuanglin Town use them to reel silk. The method is to take the cocoons and dry them in the sun, store them in a large earthenware bowl, and soak them thoroughly with boiling water. Scoop them out to draw out the thread ends, separate a cluster into the cauldron, and reel them according to the common method. When reeled halfway through, take another cluster to join and spin. The water in the cauldron does not need an active fire beneath it to keep it hot; it only needs to be slightly warm.

# Making Silk Floss

Silk floss and filament silk are equally necessary for clothing. Whenever cocoons are unsuitable for filament silk and have already been set aside, one should immediately use them to manufacture silk floss once the silk reeling is finished. Floss made from the first brood of silkworms is tough, while floss from the second brood is loose. There are also those who make it from cocoon waste <note>original: 繭絖 (jiǎnkuàng); coarse silk refuse</note>. In antiquity, people only began to wear silk garments at age fifty. Today, the people of Huzhou, young and old alike, all rely on this floss to ward off cold. Its lightweight warmth and comfortable fit far surpass tree cotton <term>木棉</term> <gloss>kapok or plant cotton</gloss>.

Also multiply 6 men by 48 *chi* to obtain 288 *chi*.

Combine them to obtain 932 *chi*, which serves as the divisor <term>fa</term> <note>original: 法 (*fa*); the divisor in traditional Chinese division.</note>.

Set down the cloth: 125,820 *chi*.

Then multiply the 6 men and 7 men together to obtain 42. Multiply this by the total cloth to obtain 5,284,440, which serves as the dividend <term>shi</term> <note>original: 實 (*shi*); the dividend in traditional Chinese division.</note>.

Divide this by the divisor to obtain the soldier count: 5,670 men each.

Multiply this by 48 and apply the division by seven rule <note>original: 七歸 (*qi gui*); standard abacus reduction rule for dividing by 7.</note> to obtain the trousers cloth.

Also multiply the soldier count by 92 and apply the division by six rule <note>original: 六歸 (*liu gui*); standard abacus reduction rule for dividing by 6.</note> to obtain the coat cloth. This matches the question.

Now suppose there are three brothers. The youngest brother says to the eldest brother: "My age compared to yours is three-fourths. The second brother's age compared to yours is five-sixths, which is eight years more than mine." One asks: what is the age of each of the three men?

The answer states:
The eldest brother is 96 years old.
The second brother is 80 years old.
The youngest brother is 72 years old.
